title: Fixed-Capacity LRU Cache (No Dynamic Allocation)
statement:
A calibration lookup, a decoded-message cache, a small pool of open file
handles -- anything with a fixed, small capacity and a "keep what was used
recently, discard what was not" policy is an **LRU cache**. On a hosted
platform you would reach for a hash map plus a linked list from the standard
library and move on. On an embedded target there usually is no heap
allocator you are allowed to call after start-up, so both of those have to
be built from a couple of fixed-size arrays instead -- and it is in that
translation that this problem gets fiendish.

## The data structure

```
#define LRU_MAX_CAPACITY 8

typedef struct {
    int32_t capacity;
    int32_t count;
    int32_t mru;                      /* slot index of the most-recently-used
                                          entry, or -1 if the cache is empty */
    int32_t lru;                      /* slot index of the least-recently-used
                                          entry, or -1 if the cache is empty */
    int32_t key[LRU_MAX_CAPACITY];
    int32_t value[LRU_MAX_CAPACITY];
    int32_t prev[LRU_MAX_CAPACITY];   /* toward the LRU end, -1 if none */
    int32_t next[LRU_MAX_CAPACITY];   /* toward the MRU end, -1 if none */
} LruCache;
```

`key`/`value`/`prev`/`next` are an **intrusive doubly linked list threaded
through array indices instead of pointers** -- slot `i`'s neighbours in
recency order are `prev[i]` and `next[i]`, not addresses. This is the
standard shape for a fixed-capacity cache with no `malloc`: `capacity` never
exceeds `LRU_MAX_CAPACITY`, so the arrays are sized once, at compile time,
and every operation is a matter of relinking a handful of integers rather
than moving memory around.

## Your functions

```
void    lru_init(LruCache *cache, int32_t capacity);
int32_t lru_get(LruCache *cache, int32_t key);
void    lru_put(LruCache *cache, int32_t key, int32_t value);
```

- `lru_init` resets `cache` to empty with the given `capacity`
  (`1 <= capacity <= LRU_MAX_CAPACITY`, guaranteed by every test).
- `lru_get` returns the value stored for `key`, or `-1` if `key` is not
  present. **A successful lookup counts as a use** -- it must make `key`
  the most-recently-used entry, same as a `put` would.
- `lru_put` stores `value` under `key`. If `key` is already present, its
  value is updated (not duplicated) and it becomes most-recently-used. If
  `key` is new and the cache is already at `capacity`, the current
  **least**-recently-used entry is evicted to make room. Stored values are
  never negative, which is what lets `-1` unambiguously mean "not found".

## Watch out

- **A cache hit on `lru_get` has to move the entry, not just read it.**
  It is easy to write a `get` that only searches and returns, because
  nothing about "look this up" sounds like it should mutate anything --
  but the recency order *is* the cache's state, and reading an entry
  without refreshing its position means the next eviction can throw away
  something that was just used.
- **`lru_put` on a key that already exists must not touch `count` or evict
  anything.** It is an update-in-place plus a recency touch, not an insert
  -- growing `count` for a key that was already counted corrupts every
  eviction decision made after it.
- **Eviction reuses the evicted slot's own index for the new entry**, it
  does not claim a fresh one -- there is no fresh one to claim once
  `count` has reached `capacity`. Detaching the old least-recently-used
  slot from the list, before overwriting its key and value and re-inserting
  it at the most-recently-used end, has to happen in an order that leaves
  `cache->lru` and `cache->mru` correct at every intermediate step, not
  just at the end.
- **`capacity == 1` is a real, tested case**, not a degenerate one to
  special-case away: every `put` evicts whatever was there a moment ago,
  and the single surviving slot has to end up as both `mru` and `lru` of
  itself again afterwards.
- Detaching a slot from the *middle* of the list means fixing up **two**
  neighbours, not one -- the slot on either side of it needs its `next` or
  `prev` repointed around the gap. Getting only one side right passes
  every test where the touched slot happens to already be at an end of the
  list, and fails the moment it is not.

tests.name: basic put and get, no eviction
a full cache evicts the true least-recently-used key
tests.stdin:
2
PUT 1 10
PUT 2 20
PUT 3 30
GET 1
GET 2
GET 3
tests.description: Key 1 was inserted first and never touched again, so it is the one evicted when key 3 needs room.

tests.name: a get refreshes recency and changes which key gets evicted
tests.stdin:
2
PUT 1 10
PUT 2 20
GET 1
PUT 3 30
GET 1
GET 2
GET 3
tests.description: Reading key 1 makes key 2 the least-recently-used one, so key 2 is evicted instead of key 1 when key 3 arrives -- the opposite of the previous test.

tests.name: put on an existing key updates it and counts as a touch
tests.stdin:
2
PUT 1 10
PUT 2 20
PUT 1 11
PUT 3 30
GET 1
GET 2
GET 3
tests.description: Re-putting key 1 updates its value to 11 and moves it to most-recently-used, so key 2 -- not key 1 -- is what key 3's insertion evicts.

tests.name: capacity 1: every put evicts whatever was just there
a stored value of 0 is not confused with a miss
